The combined effect of the Route 680 and Jackson Avenue/Alum Rock Avenue noise in the northeasterly corner of the neighborhood result in Ldn noise levels of 70-80 extending from westerly of Jackson Avenue to the freeway right-of-way. In addition to Jackson Avenue, Alum Rock Avenue, San Antonio Street, and King Road all contribute measurable noise to the Mayfair CNRA. In each instance, Ldn levels of 70-80 occur within the street right-of-way, with levels of Ldn 60-70 extending approximately 150 feet on both sides of the roadway.
Northside CNRA:
Noise affects the westerly and easterly portions of Northside. The combination of the Western Pacific railroad line and Bayshore Freeway produce a broad zone of noise, with Ldn 70-80 contours along both transportation corridors, and Ldn 60-70 contours bulging out approximately 500 feet each side of the freeway and approximately 100 feet from the rail line. High noise conditions also prevail along the Southern Pacific Railroad line in the northwesterly corner of the neighborhood and along Taylor Street easterly to 13th Street, and along 13th Street through the area. In these areas the Ldn 70-80 is limited to the street or rail right-of-way with the Ldn 60-70 contour extending an additional 100-200 feet beyond.
The <u>Noise Element</u> projects that by 1995 additional vehicular traffic through the Northside neighborhood will create Ldn 70-80 on Taylor Street from 13th Street to the freeway, along Julian Street, and along 17th Street between Taylor and Julian Streets. Noise levels of Ldn 60-70 is projected to be experienced approximately 100-200 feet beyond the Ldn 70-80 level along each of these thoroughfares.
Olinder CNRA:
At the time of the <u>Noise Element</u> measurements (1974) both Santa Clara Street and the Western Pacific rail line were in the Ldn 70-80 contours, with Ldn 60-70 contours paralleling each in a band approximately 200 feet wide. Noise projections for 1995 indicate Ldn 70-80 levels along 24th Street through Olinder with Ldn 60-70 noise levels parallel and approximately 100 feet westerly of the street.
H. URBAN DESIGN
This discussion should begin by noting that apparently there exists no authoritative source document relating specifically to the historical development of San Jose's urban form. Assuming San Jose's settlement was comparable to that of the rest of California, the year 1870 would have found the framework for San Jose's future urban form already developing. "In keeping with the established American procedure, the towns which came into existence in the 1860's and 1870's...were usually laid out by a small-time speculator hoping to take advantage of some nearby installation: A railroad stop, a ferry, a bill . . ." In San Jose, both railroad and ferry were present: The Southern Pacific tracks and depot dated from 1864; and the Alviso steamship service to San Francisco had operated since 1849. For these mid-nineteenth century towns, "A grid was the inevitable pattern of house lots and streets . . ." The grid had by 1870 become "a well-established American tradition."
